claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has a naturally formed native oxide layer.
The corrosion resistance of pre-exposure Q235 steel in harsh chloride environments is governed by the integrity of its native oxide layer.
Elevating the exposure temperature to about 80°C enhances metal or metal-ion diffusion in Q235 steel or its surface film.
Enhanced diffusion at elevated temperature promotes repair of the native oxide film.
Enhanced diffusion at elevated temperature produces a more continuous, dense, and adherent oxide film.
Limited diffusivity at room temperature produces a more porous and defective oxide film.
A porous and defective oxide film provides inferior protection against localized corrosion.
Q235 specimens exposed at about 80°C will form a more uniform and protective oxide layer than specimens exposed at about 25°C.
Q235 specimens exposed at about 80°C will have lower corrosion current density than specimens exposed at about 25°C.
Q235 specimens exposed at about 80°C will exhibit fewer localized-corrosion features than specimens exposed at about 25°C.
Q235 specimens exposed at about 80°C will have lower corrosion-related mass loss than specimens exposed at about 25°C.
The proposed protective effect applies around 80°C in chloride-rich conditions.
At extreme temperatures or under substantially different environmental chemistries, other corrosion mechanisms may become dominant.
Thermal stress-induced cracking may counteract any improvement in oxide integrity caused by elevated-temperature diffusion.
